claims.claim: The reader who proposed the Urth list's chapter-by-chapter close reading says he does not believe in trivial trivia in Wolfe.
claims.quote: I don't believe in trivial trivia, provided one can ask

claims.claim: The same reader describes his reading posture as walking through Wolfe like a minefield.
claims.quote: why I walk through Wolfe like a minefield

claims.claim: The same reader treats the hedge word “perhaps” in Severian's narration as a signal that something is being covered.
claims.quote: uses a perhaps, or one of its relatives, I get nervous

claims.claim: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes calls the first line of Shadow of the Torturer a haunting first line.
claims.source: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes, Urth mailing list, 5 September 2006
claims.quote: A rather haunting first line, for me.

claims.claim: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes says the first page of Shadow of the Torturer is full of forward references.
claims.source: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes, Urth mailing list, 5 September 2006
claims.quote: This first page is full of forward

claims.claim: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes says the fight in chapter I is more like a real fight than most in fiction.
claims.source: Dan'l Danehy-Oakes, Urth mailing list, 5 September 2006
claims.quote: more like a real fight than most in fiction.
claims.page: message body, note on the fight

claims.quote: Not Vodalus', to be sure; so the magickal explanation he

claims.feature: other: counter-evidence, anomaly as authorial error
claims.claim: Roy C. Lackey argues that a contradiction about who was handed the pistol, repeated in the appendix to Citadel of the Autarch, is probably Wolfe's own mistake rather than the narrator's.
claims.source: Roy C. Lackey, Urth mailing list, 5 September 2006
claims.quote: so the mistake is probably Wolfe's.

claims.claim: Gevers says each volume of The Book of the Long Sun opens with a dialogue in which the informed figure yields his information only in oracular or otherwise obscure form.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: which he will only yield up in oracular or otherwise obscure form

claims.claim: Gevers says the information in each opening passage, and the precise character of its obscurity, amount to terms of reading for the rest of the volume.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: amount to guidance, to terms of reading, for the remainder

claims.claim: Gevers, using Kim Stanley Robinson's and John Clute's term 'slingshot ending', describes an ending whose momentum of implication carries beyond the text it terminates.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000, citing Kim Stanley Robinson and John Clute
claims.quote: an ending whose momentum of implication carries well beyond the confines

claims.claim: Gevers reads the first words of Lake of the Long Sun as establishing that silent implication can convey as much as any violent confrontation.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: silent implication can convey as much as any violent confrontation
claims.page: section on Lake of the Long Sun's opening

claims.claim: Gevers says the opening of Nightside the Long Sun presents signs to two augurs at once, Silk and the reader.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: signs are presented to those augurs, Silk and the reader
claims.page: section on Nightside the Long Sun's opening

claims.claim: Gevers reads a passing description of a boy's frozen grin as an ironic tribute to that character's concealed function as the tetralogy's narrator.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: his craftily concealed and long-term function as Long Sun
claims.page: section on Nightside the Long Sun's opening

claims.claim: Gevers says that in Exodus From the Long Sun Wolfe's narration becomes spare and unexplanatory, a minefield of hints and implications.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, “The Reader as Augur”, Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: narration becomes spare, unexplanatory, a minefield of hints and implications
claims.page: section on Exodus From the Long Sun
